cells.tense: You're here in it, hands on the work, no hurry in them.
cells.ask: Add one more repetition than feels tidy, then stop clean and leave it stopped.
cells.core:
The practice runs and it doesn't run you. You show up, you refine what's in front of you, you put it down when it's done — and putting it down doesn't feel like losing anything. In a spot where things are already finishing, that steadiness keeps a corner of your life whole and yours.

What's still moving through the endings doesn't need your grip on it. A small thing kept lit through repetition — that's what steadies the ground here, not pushing. Finish one thing today and let it stay finished; the next clearing is free to happen, and you get to see what your hands do when they're not holding anything up.

cells.tense: You're out ahead of yourself, bracing for a version of this that hasn't arrived.
cells.ask: Let one loose end stay loose tonight — no tidying, no fixing — and watch what holds without you.
cells.core:
Doing this well looks like steady hours and a clean stop — you sit down, you work, you finish, and the finishing doesn't spook you. What's happening instead is another pass, then another, and the ending stops being something you're meeting and becomes something you're managing before it happens. Solitude that used to open things now just keeps the door closed.

The release that comes from finishing is the release that's missing. Pick one thing that's actually done and set it down where you can see it. Setting it down is what makes room for the next thing; the space you get back isn't one you had to build.

cells.tense: You're still standing at a door that already shut behind you, deciding whether to knock.
cells.ask: Pick one thing that came out even — you gave, you got — and say it out loud as finished.
cells.core:
When the practice is steady it's quiet and regular: you know when the work is done because you're in it, not watching it from outside. From where you're standing now it won't take hold — you can describe steady work, you just can't get into it — and the ending sits half-cleared, waiting on you to show up.

Start where the scale is already level. A fair exchange is one you can read without running the numbers over and over: find something that ended even, name it out loud, and let that be the whole of it today. It hands back a small patch of solid ground you can stand on.

cells.tense: You're already inside the practice — pen moving, hands busy — and telling yourself you're only watching.
cells.ask: Name one thing you're good at and trace it to the hours that built it — say the hours out loud, once.
cells.core:
When this runs clean, the hours are visible and so is the choice: you sat down, you repeated, you got better, and you know you did. What's showing up instead is skill without anyone claiming it — better than before, no hours, no repetition, no decision — while the endings around you get cleared by someone who won't sign the clearing.

Enough light for the next step is all this needs. Pick one skill and say where it came from: the actual evenings, the actual repetitions. Say them out loud and the claim comes back with the words, and the ending gets something real to stand on.
